title: Mean vs median
explanation: That value is the median — the middle of the sorted list. The mean shares the total out equally: add every value, then divide by how many values there are.
microLesson: Sort 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. The middle value (median) is 4. The mean is (2+4+4+6+9)/5 = 25/5 = 5. They answer different questions: the median is the middle position; the mean is the balance point.

title: Divide by the count
explanation: You found the total. The mean is the total divided by the number of values — the last step turns a sum into an average.
microLesson: Mean = total / count. If the total catch is 25 fish over 5 days, the mean is 25 / 5 = 5 fish per day.

title: Percent and decimal are two costumes for one number
explanation: 0.30 and 30% are the same quantity in different forms. Multiply a decimal by 100 to speak in percent; divide a percent by 100 to get the decimal.
microLesson: Percent means 'per hundred'. 30% = 30/100 = 0.30. When a question asks for a percent, answer on the 0–100 scale; when it asks for a proportion, answer on the 0–1 scale.

title: Part over whole
explanation: A fraction of a group is part / whole. Put the part on top and the whole underneath — 3 of 12 boats is 3/12, not 12/3.
microLesson: Ask: out of how many in total? That total is the denominator. The count you care about is the numerator.

title: Outliers pull the mean
explanation: The mean is the balance point of the data, so one extreme value drags it toward itself. The median only cares about position, so it barely moves.
microLesson: Incomes 30, 32, 35, 38, 900 (thousands): the median is 35, but the mean jumps to 207. The single huge value moved the mean far more than the median.

title: Read the axes before the bars
explanation: Charts answer questions only after you know what each axis measures. Check the axis labels and units first, then find the bar or point.
microLesson: Habit for every chart: 1) read the title, 2) read both axis labels and units, 3) only then compare bars or points.

title: Association is not proof of cause
explanation: Two things rising together does not show one causes the other — a third factor or coincidence can produce the same pattern.
microLesson: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together every summer. Neither causes the other; hot weather drives both. To claim cause, you need an experiment or a design that rules out other explanations.

title: Which number goes on which axis
explanation: You placed the two numbers the right way round for each other, but on the wrong axes. A coordinate is written (across, up): the FIRST number moves you along the bottom axis, the SECOND moves you up the side axis.
microLesson: Read (4, 6) as: go across to 4 on the bottom axis, then up to 6 on the side axis. Swapping them lands you at (6, 4), a different place entirely. A useful phrase: along the corridor, then up the stairs.

title: Digits do not make a variable numerical
explanation: A variable is numerical only when its values are quantities you could sensibly add or average. Boat numbers are written with digits, but boat 7 is not 'more' than boat 3 — the digits are just names, so it is a categorical variable.
microLesson: Ask: would adding two of these values mean anything? Adding two catches (4 fish + 6 fish = 10 fish) is meaningful, so catch is numerical. Adding two boat numbers (boat 3 + boat 7) is meaningless, so boat number is categorical. Postcodes, shirt numbers and phone numbers are all categorical for the same reason.

title: A count does not depend on where you start
explanation: Counting pairs one number with each item, and each item is used exactly once. Nothing was added to the row or removed from it between your two passes, so the two totals cannot both be right — one pass skipped an item or counted one twice.
microLesson: Two habits fix this. First, move in one direction and touch or mark each item as you say its number, so you can see where you have reached. Second, group as you go: put the items into rows of five, count the rows in fives, then add the leftovers. Grouping means a slip costs you one group to recount, not the whole row.

title: The ten has to go somewhere
explanation: A column can only hold one digit. When the units add to more than nine, the ten inside that answer belongs in the tens column — writing only the units digit throws it away, which is why the answer comes out ten short.
microLesson: Take 47 + 38. The units are 7 + 8 = 15. That is 1 ten and 5 units: write the 5 under the units, and carry the 1 ten to the top of the tens column. The tens are now 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, so the answer is 85 — not 75. A quick check catches the slip every time: 47 is nearly 50 and 38 is nearly 40, so the answer should be near 90.

title: Borrow a ten instead of flipping the digits
explanation: In a subtraction column the top digit is what you have and the bottom digit is what you are taking away. When the top digit is smaller you cannot swap them round — that answers a different question. You borrow a ten from the next column instead.
microLesson: Take 52 - 27. The units column asks for 2 take away 7, which cannot be done as it stands. Borrow one of the 5 tens: the units become 12, and the tens drop to 4. Now 12 - 7 = 5 and 4 - 2 = 2, giving 25. Flipping the units to 7 - 2 gives 35, which is ten too big — and a rough check says 52 - 27 should be about 25.

title: Multiplying counts groups, not the two numbers
explanation: Adding the two numbers together answers 'how many altogether if I combine these two amounts'. Multiplying answers something else: how many there are when you have that many equal groups of that size. 7 x 4 is seven groups of four, which is 28, not 11.
microLesson: Write it out the long way and count what you get: 7 x 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 28. Adding gives 7 + 4 = 11, which is what you would get from one group of seven and one group of four — a different situation entirely. A sanity check: multiplying by anything above 1 makes the number bigger than either of the two numbers you started with.

title: The amount being shared goes first
explanation: Division is not like addition or multiplication — the order matters. The thing being shared out is written first, and the number of parts it is shared between is written second. Reversing them asks how much of a boat each crate gets.
microLesson: Forty crates between 8 boats is 40 / 8 = 5 crates each. Written the other way round, 8 / 40 asks how much of a boat belongs to each crate, which is a different question and gives an answer smaller than one. Before dividing, name the two roles out loud: 'the crates are being shared, the boats are sharing them.' If each part should end up with several of something, an answer below one means the two numbers went in the wrong order.

title: A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces
explanation: The bottom number of a fraction counts how many equal pieces the whole was cut into — it does not measure how much you have. Cutting the same whole into more pieces makes every piece smaller, so 1/8 is less than 1/4 even though 8 is more than 4.
microLesson: Picture two identical loaves. Cut one into 4 slices and the other into 8. A slice from the second loaf is visibly thinner, and eight thin slices are needed to rebuild what four thick ones did. This is the sharing idea from the division lesson seen from the other side: the same amount split more ways gives each share less. When the top numbers match, the fraction with the SMALLER bottom number is the larger amount.

title: Compare the columns, not the length
explanation: A decimal is not longer-is-bigger. Each column after the point is worth a tenth of the one before it, so the tenths column decides the comparison before the hundredths column gets a say. 0.5 is larger than 0.25 because 5 tenths beats 2 tenths.
microLesson: Give both numbers the same columns by padding with zeros, then read left to right. 0.5 becomes 0.50; against 0.25 the tenths are 5 against 2, so 0.50 wins and you never need the hundredths. The same trick settles 0.09 against 0.2: pad to 0.09 and 0.20, and the tenths are 0 against 2. Always pad first, then compare one column at a time.

title: Add the parts before you name a share
explanation: In a ratio, the second number counts the other ingredient — not the whole mixture. To say what fraction of the mix one ingredient is, first add every part together to find the size of the whole.
microLesson: A mix of 3 parts salt to 5 parts water has 3 and 5 make 8 parts in it altogether. The salt is 3 of those 8 parts, so 3/8 of the mix, not 3/5. The clue that something has gone wrong: the two shares must add up to the whole mixture, and 3/5 for salt plus 5/5 for water is more than one whole batch. Ratio compares part with part; a fraction compares part with whole.

title: Scale by multiplying, not by adding
explanation: Two amounts stay in proportion when one is always the same number of times the other. Adding the same amount to both keeps their difference fixed instead of their rate, which quietly changes the answer.
microLesson: If 2 crates cost 6 coins, the rate is 3 coins per crate. For 4 crates, double both: 4 crates cost 12 coins, still 3 coins each. Adding 2 to each instead would give 4 crates for 8 coins, which is 2 coins each — a different price. The check that catches it every time: work out the rate at the end and see whether it matches the rate you started with.

title: The minus sign says which way, the digits say how far
explanation: A negative number's digits measure its distance from zero; the minus sign says it lies below zero. So the further a negative number is from zero, the SMALLER it is. -12 has fallen twelve steps below zero and -7 only seven, which makes -7 the larger of the two.
microLesson: Draw the line and put zero in the middle. Positives run right and negatives run left, and the rule never changes: whatever is further left is smaller. That is why -1 is warmer than -20 on a thermometer, and why a debt of 50 leaves you worse off than a debt of 5. Comparing two negatives is the one place where the bigger-looking digits belong to the smaller number.

title: Find out what one mark is worth before you count
explanation: Marks on a rule are not always worth one unit. Counting them as if they were gives an answer that is a neat fraction of the right one — half of it when the marks are worth 2, a fifth when they are worth 5 — which is why the mistake is easy to miss.
microLesson: Two labelled values are all you need. If the rule reads 0 at one label and 10 at the next, and there are five marks between them, then each mark is worth 2. Work that out first, then count in twos rather than ones. A quick sanity check: your answer should sit between the two labels you counted from, not somewhere below both of them.

title: Name the row and the column before reading the number
explanation: A cell is fixed by two things at once: which row it sits in and which column. Landing on the right row is only half of it — the values beside each other on that row measure completely different things, so reading the wrong one answers a different question with a number that looks perfectly plausible.
microLesson: Say both out loud before you read anything: 'Thursday, crates landed.' Then find the Thursday row, run a finger across to the crates column, and read where they meet. The habit costs a second and catches the slip every time, because the mistake never announces itself — 4 boats and 18 crates are both just numbers on Thursday's row.

title: A header is not a variable
explanation: A column earns the name variable only if its values actually differ between cases. One that reads the same on every row states a fact about the whole dataset rather than about any case in it, so it can never explain why one case differs from another.
microLesson: Run your eye down the column and ask one question: do the values ever change? Harbour name reading Kirkwall on all seven rows tells you where the data came from — useful to know, useless for comparing the days, because every day shares it. The same goes for a survey where all 200 respondents answer 'dockworker'. Agreement is not strength: a column with no variation separates nobody from anybody.

title: Count rows for cases, cells for observations
explanation: Cases and observations are different counts answering different questions. The number of cases is the number of rows — the things you measured. The number of observations is the number of values recorded, which is rows times columns. Adding a column adds observations without adding a single case.
microLesson: Start every dataset by asking what one row represents. A ledger with one row per boat over 12 boats and 4 columns holds 12 cases and 48 observations. Watch for the trap where a row is not what it first seems: if the ledger has one row per delivery and some boats delivered three times, the case is a delivery, and counting rows would badly overcount the boats.

title: A frequency counts cases, not categories
explanation: That number is how many different values the variable can take, not how many cases took one of them. A frequency answers 'how many of the things I measured fell in this group', so the count you want is a count of rows in the log, not a count of the words the log uses.
microLesson: A log of 20 mornings using the words calm, choppy and rough has 3 categories and 20 cases. The frequency of rough is the number of mornings written rough - 4 of them - not the 3 words available. Point at each morning in turn and count only the ones you want; the answer can never be larger than the number of cases.

title: Count every value before naming a mode
explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often, which you cannot know until you have counted them all. Stopping at the first repeat finds a value that repeats, not the one that repeats most - and it hides the case where two values tie, which is a real and common shape for data to have.
microLesson: Take 3, 6, 3, 9, 6, 4, 3, 6. Reading left to right, 3 repeats first. But finish the count: 3 appears three times and 6 appears three times too. Both are modes; the set is bimodal. A dataset can have one mode, two, several, or none at all when every value appears exactly once.

title: Skew is named after the tail, not the crowd
explanation: Looking at where most of the data sits is the natural thing to do, and it gives the wrong name every time, because the convention points at the thin end rather than the thick one. A distribution is right-skewed when its long tail stretches to the right, which is also when most of its values are packed to the left. The crowd and the name always sit on opposite sides.
microLesson: Take a berth log: waits of 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9 and one of 90 minutes. Six readings are packed low and one stretches far to the high side. The tail runs right, so the set is right-skewed - even though every value but one sits on the left. Check it against the summaries: the mean is 18.71 and the median is 7, and a mean above the median is the signature of a right tail.
